info.name: Ward Vitals Lab — Grafana API
info.description:
Beginner walkthrough of the Grafana REST API for the Ward Vitals lab.

This lab has no REST API of its own: Telegraf writes to Postgres and
TimescaleDB over the wire protocol (not HTTP). The HTTP surface you can
test in Postman is Grafana's own API on http://localhost:3000.

How to use this collection
  1. Import the companion environment (postman/postman_environment.json),
     set it Active, and fill in adminUser / adminPassword from your repo's
     .env file (GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER / GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD).
  2. Run the requests top-to-bottom. Each one teaches one small idea and
     has a Tests script that turns green only when the response is right.
  3. Requests 01-06 are read-only. Requests 07-10 create and then delete a
     temporary service account, so nothing permanent is left behind.

What you'll see in order
  01 no-auth call           02 basic auth           03 read datasources
  04 find the dashboard     05 fetch dashboard JSON 06 live SQL->TimescaleDB
  07 create service account 08 mint API token       09 bearer auth
  10 cleanup

The 'auth ladder' 01 -> 02 -> 09 is the main idea: a public health endpoint,
then password auth, then a scoped machine token.

Dataset gotcha: the simulated ward ranges roughly 2026-01-01 .. 2026-02-01
(live tail keeps advancing). Query 'now()' last-N-hours windows and you get
nothing; request 06 deliberately reads the newest hour present instead.

See docs/postman.md for the full beginner guide.

request.description:
The only request with no auth at all. Every other call needs a
credential of some kind. `/api/health` is deliberately public so monitoring
tools can check Grafana is alive before logging in.

Press Send. The Tests tab (green check to the right of the response) should
show 2 passing tests and the Console can show the version.

Expected: 200 with { \"database\": \"ok\", \"version\": \"13.0.2\", ... }

exec: pm.test("we are logged in as a Grafana admin", () => pm.expect(who.isGrafanaAdmin).to.eql(true));
console.log("Logged in as \"" + who.login + "\" orgId=" + who.orgId);

request.description:
First call WITH credentials. Postman sends an Authorization header
automatically because you configured Basic auth here, using the environment
variables {{adminUser}} and {{adminPassword}}.

Inspect the Authorization section on the request tab to see the two {{ }}
placeholders - Postman swaps in the Active environment's values at send time.

Expected: 200 with your Grafana admin info and \"isGrafanaAdmin\": true.
If this fails with 401, open the collection's eye icon (top right), select
the environment, and confirm adminUser / adminPassword match your .env.

exec: pm.test("TimescaleDB datasource is present (uid \"timescale\")", () => pm.expect(ds.some(d => d.uid === "timescale")).to.eql(true));

request.description:
Lists every data source Grafana knows about. There is exactly one: the
provisioned TimescaleDB/PostgreSQL datasource with uid \"timescale\" that
points at the timescaledb service on port 5432. This is the connection that
will later execute SQL on your behalf in request 06.

Expected: 200 with an array whose first element has
\"type\": \"grafana-postgresql-datasource\" and \"uid\": \"timescale\".

exec: pm.test("the Ward Vitals dashboard is indexed", () => pm.expect(hits.some(h => h.uid === "ward-vitals")).to.eql(true));

request.description:
Searches Grafana's index. The query parameter ?type=dash-db narrows the
search to dashboards only. This is how an external tool would discover what
dashboards exist before asking for one by uid.

Expected: 200 with an array that includes an entry \"uid\": \"ward-vitals\".

Fetches the full dashboard definition as JSON: the same shape the UI uses
internally. Everything a dashboard is - panels, queries, variables - is
machine-readable, which is why dashboards can live in git.

Expected: 200 with \"dashboard\".\"title\" == \"Ward Vitals\" and its panels list.

exec: pm.test("SQL executed and returned rows", () => pm.expect(frame && frame.data.values.length > 0 && frame.data.values[0].length > 0).to.eql(true));

request.description:
The payoff: POST a SQL string and Grafana proxies it to TimescaleDB for
you. The body says \"query datasource uid=timescale, run this rawSql".

The query is written so it ALWAYS has data regardless of when you run it:
it aggregates the newest hour present in `vitals`, using
`WHERE time = (SELECT max(time) FROM vitals)`. The lab's simulated clock
ticks forward from ~2026-02-01, so 'now()' queries would come back empty.

Expected: 200 with results.A.status == 200 and one frame whose values carry
the timestamp, an hourly average heart rate, and a row count.
Try editing rawSql in the Body tab to a query of your own - that is the
whole point of this request.

exec: pm.test("named postman-lab with Viewer role", () => pm.expect(sa.name === "postman-lab" && sa.role === "Viewer").to.eql(true));
console.log("Service account id " + sa.id + " (saved to serviceAccountId)");

request.description:
Machines shouldn't log in with your human password; they get a dedicated
identity. A service account is that identity in Grafana.

This POST creates one named postman-lab with the read-only Viewer role.
It mutates Grafana, so it only appears when you run the collection - and
request 10 deletes it again, leaving the instance exactly as it was.

The response's id is captured by the test script into the environment
variable serviceAccountId so request 08 can use it.

Expected: 201 with {\"name\": \"postman-lab\", \"role\": \"Viewer\", \"id\": ...}.

item.name: 08 · Mint an API token for that account

exec: pm.test("token looks like a Grafana glsa_ token", () => pm.expect(String(tok.token)).to.match(/^glsa_/));
console.log("Token saved to environment variable scopedToken - request 09 uses it.");

request.description:
A service account alone can't authenticate - it needs an API token.
This POST issues one (glsa_...) against the account created in 07, using
{{serviceAccountId}} written by that request's test.

The token is a secret: Postman stores it in the scopedToken environmental
variable where it is masked (•••). It is shown to you exactly once by
the API by design.

Expected: 200 with \"token\": \"glsa_...\" and the account id of 07.

exec: pm.test("we see the main org as a Viewer", () => pm.expect(orgs.map(o => o.id)).to.include(1));
console.log("Authenticated via scoped token, not the admin password.");
console.log("Cleaned up. The instance is back to its pre-collection state.");

request.description:
Tidies up the identity created in 07/08 and clears the environment
variables so no token lingers. Run this whenever you finish.

Expected: 200/204 with a confirmation message.
